paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly LogitBoost, MART, and a related variant improve their optimization objectives. It treats these methods within a common framework: they build an additive collection of regression trees, use logistic loss to measure prediction errors, and optimize through boosting. This shared view makes it possible to compare the consequences of their different update choices.

The analysis introduces a new formulation of weak learnability, the condition underlying its convergence results. Under this formulation, using only gradient descent yields an O(1/T) convergence rate, where T represents the number of iterations. Using Newton descent instead gives a linear convergence rate, meaning that the remaining optimization gap contracts geometrically rather than decreasing inversely with the iteration count.

The analysis further distinguishes where Newton descent enters the procedure. Incorporating it while growing trees, as LogitBoost does, produces a faster linear rate. Experiments on UCI datasets support these theoretical comparisons. The findings connect specific optimization choices to convergence speed under the paper’s formulation.
icml-2014-a-convergence-rate-analysis-fo.tldr: Under a new weak learnability formulation, Newton updates give faster convergence guarantees for tree boosting than gradient updates alone.

paragraphs: Learning to act in a physical environment requires a model of how that environment changes. For robots interacting with multiple objects, the challenge includes representing those interactions compactly enough to support learning. The paper argues that existing relational representations capture relationships among objects but are insufficiently compact for practical robotics.

The proposed approach uses physics as a starting point for the model. It draws on simulation tools to parameterize physical dynamics efficiently, giving the learner a structured description of how objects can behave. This acts as an inductive bias: the representation favors dynamics consistent with its physical assumptions, shaping the models the learner considers.

The reported results show that this representation can substantially accelerate learning in physical environments. The explanation offered is that its strong bias is appropriate for those environments, so the structure helps the learner use experience more effectively. The contribution therefore links a compact representation of dynamics with faster learning when the physical assumptions fit the setting.
icml-2014-a-physics-based-model-prior-fo.tldr: A compact dynamics model built around physics simulations can accelerate reinforcement learning when its physical assumptions suit the environment.

paragraphs: Supervised embedding models represent features and labels in ways that support tasks such as ranking, recommendation, and annotation. Existing linear approaches can handle large datasets successfully. The authors nevertheless argue that their linear structure may prevent them from fully exploiting additional data, and suggest that these models commonly underfit.

Affinity Weighted Embedding introduces a family of models that changes how individual embedding components contribute. Each component associated with features and labels is reweighted by an affinity function, which may be nonlinear. This adds flexibility to the relationship between features and labels while retaining the embedding framework that made earlier methods useful.

The paper describes several variants and demonstrates usefulness across several datasets. Its central idea is to enrich an embedding through the weights placed on its components. The stated aim is better predictive performance while preserving many benefits of existing embedding models. The evidence supports the usefulness of this design family; the claim that linear predecessors typically underfit remains the authors’ motivating assessment.
icml-2014-affinity-weighted-embedding-3e.tldr: Affinity Weighted Embedding adds potentially nonlinear component weights to supervised embeddings, with useful results across several datasets.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a generative autoencoder that learns multiple levels of distributed representations. Its hidden layers are stochastic, so they describe uncertain internal variables rather than only deterministic transformations. Autoregressive connections organize dependencies within successive hidden layers, providing a structure for generating values in a defined sequence.

That structure allows fast, exact ancestral sampling from the model. Sampling and learning have different computational properties here: although generation is exact, parameter estimation uses an efficient approximation. The training method follows the minimum description length principle and can also be understood as maximizing a variational lower bound on log-likelihood.

A feedforward neural network supplies approximate inference, helping estimate hidden representations from observed data during learning. Together, these components connect hierarchical representation learning, tractable generation, and approximate training within one model. The authors report state-of-the-art generative performance on several UCI datasets, MNIST, and Atari 2600 games. These findings support the model’s effectiveness across the evaluated datasets while preserving the distinction between exact sampling and approximate inference.
icml-2014-deep-autoregressive-networks-2.tldr: Deep autoregressive networks combine hierarchical stochastic representations, exact sampling, and approximate training, with strong reported generative performance.

paragraphs: DeepBoost is an ensemble learning algorithm designed to use expressive base classifiers, including deep decision trees and other complex model families. Such flexibility makes the selection of ensemble members especially important. The paper’s central proposal is a selection criterion that accounts for model capacity while pursuing predictive accuracy.

The theoretical contribution consists of data-dependent learning bounds for convex ensembles. These bounds incorporate the Rademacher complexities of the different classifier subfamilies, together with the mixture weight each subfamily receives. In plain language, the analysis considers both how flexible the available families are and how heavily the ensemble relies on each one.

DeepBoost seeks to minimize the corresponding learning bound, connecting its selection procedure directly to the theory. The authors report that the method can achieve high accuracy without overfitting and present experiments comparing favorably with AdaBoost, logistic regression, and their L1-regularized versions. The contribution is a principled way to use rich classifier families while explicitly accounting for their capacity during ensemble construction.
icml-2014-deep-boosting-dafb74cde8.tldr: DeepBoost selects expressive ensemble members using a capacity-aware learning bound and reports favorable performance against several established classifiers.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification when the original observations are unavailable but summary statistics remain accessible. This situation can arise when collecting simple statistics is easy while storing all the data is impractical. The setting considered has discrete variables and access to various marginal distributions, which describe selected parts of the data distribution.

The proposed framework learns a classifier directly from this partial information. It minimizes worst-case hinge loss, using an objective that upper-bounds generalization error. This makes prediction loss central to the construction. The authors contrast it with maximum entropy approaches that reconstruct a complete distribution, which they describe as introducing conditional independence assumptions without directly optimizing prediction loss.

Computational feasibility depends on the statistics supplied. The paper identifies certain collections for which the problem is tractable and uses MAP linear programming relaxations to approximate the general case. Experiments show competitive performance against methods receiving the same information. The result offers a discriminative route from stored distribution summaries to a classifier.
icml-2014-discrete-chebyshev-classifiers.tldr: Discrete Chebyshev classifiers learn from marginal statistics by minimizing worst-case hinge loss, with tractable special cases and approximations for general cases.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms need every input to have a fixed number of features, even when the inputs are sentences or documents of different lengths. Bag-of-words representations provide one solution, but discard word order and fail to represent semantic relationships between words. These weaknesses motivate learning a richer representation of whole texts.

The proposed unsupervised algorithm assigns each document a dense vector and trains that vector to predict words appearing in the document. Prediction supplies the learning signal, allowing the representation to be learned without task labels. The construction gives the method the potential to address the weaknesses identified in bag-of-words representations.

The empirical results show better performance than bag-of-words models and other text representation methods. The authors also report new state-of-the-art results on several text classification and sentiment analysis tasks. These findings connect the word-prediction training objective to useful document features: vectors learned without task labels can support subsequent prediction tasks that depend on the content of a sentence or document.
icml-2014-distributed-representations-of.tldr: An unsupervised word-prediction objective learns dense document vectors that outperform several text representations in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Dual Query addresses the problem of answering many questions about a dataset while maintaining differential privacy. The challenge becomes computationally severe when each record has many attributes. The paper explicitly retains the unavoidable worst-case cost: its complexity can grow exponentially with the number of dimensions.

The practical contribution is to package the difficult computation into a compactly specified integer program. Standard solvers can handle this subproblem without themselves implementing a private optimization algorithm. The overall procedure has proven privacy and accuracy guarantees, so the non-private solution of that internal optimization problem is part of the analyzed private method.

Experiments show that this organization can work well despite the worst-case complexity. The authors report efficiently and accurately answering millions of queries on the Netflix dataset, which has more than 17,000 attributes, and describe an improvement of multiple orders of magnitude over the state of the art. The result demonstrates substantial practical reach without claiming to eliminate the underlying computational difficulty.
icml-2014-dual-query-practical-private-q.tldr: Dual Query uses standard integer-program solvers within a provably private algorithm to answer large query collections effectively in practice.

paragraphs: Combining multiple contributors becomes more complicated when their outputs are structured sequences rather than separate labels. This paper studies that problem through visual tracking. Each contributor supplies a sequence of bounding boxes, and the desired output is the unknown trajectory of the target object across time.

The authors propose a factorial hidden Markov model that jointly learns the target trajectory and the reliability of each tracker. Estimating these quantities together lets the aggregation account for differences among contributors while modeling the evolving target. For efficient online inference, the method uses a conditional particle filter designed around the structure of the joint posterior distribution of hidden variables.

The evaluation compares two ensemble methods built from five state-of-the-art trackers with the individual trackers on a large open visual tracking benchmark. The reported results provide encouraging empirical support for combining their strengths. The broader contribution is an aggregation method that treats contributor reliability and temporal structure as connected parts of the same estimation problem.
icml-2014-ensemble-based-tracking-aggreg.tldr: A factorial hidden Markov model combines tracking sequences by jointly estimating the target trajectory and each tracker’s reliability.

paragraphs: Structured prediction concerns outputs whose parts have relationships, making ensemble design more involved than combining isolated class decisions. This paper develops a collection of learning algorithms for constructing accurate ensembles in that setting. It pairs the algorithmic proposals with theoretical guarantees about learning.

Several methods come from converting online learning algorithms into batch procedures. Online learning updates a predictor sequentially, while a batch procedure produces a predictor from an available training collection. The paper develops new conversions for this purpose and includes both randomized and deterministic algorithms, providing multiple routes from sequential learning procedures to structured prediction ensembles.

Another contribution is a boosting-style algorithm that applies when the structured prediction setting has many labels. The authors provide a detailed study of the proposed methods and their guarantees, together with extensive experiments on several structured prediction tasks. The contribution therefore combines ensemble construction, analysis, and empirical evaluation, giving a family of approaches for learning with structured outputs rather than a single prescribed ensemble procedure.
icml-2014-ensemble-methods-for-structure.tldr: The paper develops structured prediction ensembles through new online-to-batch conversions and a boosting-style method, supported by learning guarantees and experiments.

paragraphs: Finito targets optimization problems whose objective is a finite sum of smooth, strongly convex functions. The finite-sum structure gives an optimizer information beyond access to a single undifferentiated objective. The paper builds on the idea that exploiting the individual terms can be faster than treating the entire sum as a batch problem.

The proposed incremental gradient method has a theoretical convergence rate described as four times faster than existing methods when the sum contains sufficiently many terms. Both the smoothness and strong convexity assumptions, along with the requirement on the number of terms, define the scope of this result. The rate comparison concerns optimization convergence under those conditions.

Finito also accommodates sampling without replacement, so terms can be visited without repeatedly selecting the same term within a sampling pass. The authors report that this choice gives further practical speedups. Their empirical results show state-of-the-art performance, complementing the theoretical result with evidence that the finite-sum structure and sampling strategy can translate into effective optimization.
icml-2014-finito-a-faster-permutable-inc.tldr: Finito improves the theoretical convergence rate for sufficiently large smooth, strongly convex finite sums and gains further empirical speedups from sampling without replacement.

paragraphs: The paper treats the detection of abnormal cortical tissue in epilepsy patients as an image segmentation problem. Its goal is to locate and isolate suspicious regions in MRI surface images. Each region is assessed by comparing it with the corresponding anatomical region across controls, making abnormality a regional comparison.

The method performs these comparisons at multiple scales, dividing surface images into segments of different sizes. Each segment receives an outlier probability. A tree-structured hierarchical conditional random field then combines the probabilities from the different scales to produce the final classification, bringing the separate regional assessments into one segmentation procedure.

The authors report correct detection in 90% of patients whose abnormalities had been identified through routine visual inspection of clinical MRI. They also report detecting abnormalities in 80% of patients whose abnormalities escaped expert radiologists’ visual inspection. These are results for two different patient groups. Together, they support the potential value of multiscale outlier detection for finding cortical abnormalities, including abnormalities missed during visual review.
icml-2014-hierarchical-conditional-rando.tldr: A hierarchical model combines multiscale MRI outlier scores and detects abnormalities in both visually identified and previously missed patient cases.

paragraphs: Learning a probabilistic graphical model does not automatically make it useful for answering probabilistic questions. Even when a learning algorithm is statistically consistent, inference in its output can remain computationally difficult. This paper builds the requirements of approximate inference into the learning procedure itself.

The method always returns models with high-girth graphs in the correlation decay regime. High girth means the graphs lack short cycles, while correlation decay limits the persistence of dependence across distance. For this class, approximate inference methods such as loopy belief propagation are known to produce marginal probabilities close to the model’s true marginals.

The paper also derives finite-sample guarantees: beyond a specified sample-size threshold, learned models answer probabilistic queries with high accuracy. This connects the tractability of inference within the returned model to the statistical quality of the learned answers. Synthetic-data experiments show advantages over algorithms that do not return high-girth graphs. The guarantees depend on the restricted model class that makes reliable approximate inference possible.
icml-2014-inferning-with-high-girth-grap.tldr: Learning high-girth graphical models in the correlation decay regime enables approximate inference guarantees and finite-sample guarantees for accurate probabilistic answers.

paragraphs: Human annotations can reflect differences in ability, differences in item difficulty, and recurring patterns of confusion among labels. The paper introduces a normalized gamma construction for confusion matrices that can represent all three. A confusion matrix describes which labels or judgments tend to be mistaken for others.

The authors then develop latent confusion analysis to summarize the main patterns behind many individual annotators’ judgments. Its stated assumption is that confusion matrices are shared across people. These shared patterns, called latent confusions, play a summarizing role analogous to latent topics in topic modeling.

The motivation is interpretability: inspecting a separate confusion matrix for every worker can become difficult, while a small collection of principal confusion matrices offers a more compact account. The authors apply the approach to judgments about radioactivity’s effects on fish and shellfish following the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster. The application illustrates the intended use of the framework: analyzing the structure of human confusion through shared patterns while accounting for ability and item difficulty.
icml-2014-latent-confusion-analysis-by-n.tldr: Latent confusion analysis summarizes human judgment patterns through shared confusion matrices while modeling annotator ability and item difficulty.

paragraphs: Gaussian graphical models often rely on sparsity to make high-dimensional estimation statistically and computationally manageable. Yet observed data may exhibit many dependencies, making a sparse model an inadequate description. This paper studies models in which unobserved variables help explain why the observed relationships appear dense.

The key assumption is conditional sparsity: relationships become sparse when the latent variables are taken into account, although the observed marginal model remains non-sparse. In this setting, the inverse covariance matrix has a low-rank plus sparse structure. This decomposition supports learning through regularized maximum likelihood, with the two components representing the model’s structured departure from ordinary sparsity.

The main contribution is a set of new parameter estimation error bounds for high-dimensional latent variable Gaussian graphical models under conditions described as mild. These results complement existing theory about learning model structure by addressing the accuracy of estimated parameters. The authors present them as opening possibilities for statistical inference with these models, extending the theoretical basis for using latent structure to explain dense observed dependencies.
icml-2014-learning-latent-variable-gauss.tldr: The paper derives parameter estimation error bounds for high-dimensional Gaussian graphical models whose latent variables induce low-rank plus sparse structure.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes model repulsion, making them useful when a collection should display diversity. Their usefulness depends on the kernel parameters that determine the process. Learning those parameters is difficult because the likelihood is non-convex and, in many settings, cannot feasibly be computed.

The paper proposes Bayesian methods for learning DPP kernel parameters. The methods apply to large discrete settings as well as continuous ones, broadening the situations in which the model can be fitted. A central feature is that learning can proceed even when only bounds on the likelihood are available, directly addressing the computational obstacle posed by exact likelihood evaluation.

The authors demonstrate the methods in two applications: studying diabetic neuropathy progression through the spatial distribution of nerve fibers, and studying human perceptions of diversity in images. These applications illustrate distinct uses of repulsion-based modeling. The contribution is a way to learn the parameters governing such models in settings where the likelihood itself is difficult to evaluate.
icml-2014-learning-the-parameters-of-det.tldr: Bayesian methods learn DPP kernel parameters in large discrete and continuous settings, including cases where the likelihood can only be bounded.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to design nonlinear measurements that compress high-dimensional data into fewer dimensions. It considers two goals: reconstructing the original signal from those measurements, and classifying the data directly in the compressed space. In both cases, the measurements are assumed to contain additive Gaussian noise.

The measurement functions are selected through constrained optimization of mutual information. This makes information preservation central to the design of the compressed representation. The authors derive new analytical expressions for the gradient of mutual information in this setting, allowing arbitrary input-signal statistics within the stated measurement-noise model.

The work also connects this approach to kernel methods, including support vector machines. Experiments on multiple datasets give encouraging results for both reconstruction and classification, with the nonlinear approach reported to be particularly valuable under high noise. The contribution combines a design objective, mathematical tools for optimizing it, and evidence that the resulting noisy compressed measurements can remain useful for the intended downstream task.
icml-2014-nonlinear-information-theoreti.tldr: Information-based optimization designs nonlinear compressed measurements for reconstruction and classification, with encouraging results especially in high-noise settings.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods learn how to choose actions in sequential decision problems, including high-dimensional robotics tasks. Their practical burden is often the amount of experience required to reach strong performance. This paper addresses that sample-efficiency problem by allowing knowledge gained across tasks to contribute to learning.

The authors develop a multi-task policy gradient method for tasks encountered consecutively. As the agent learns one decision-making task after another, the method transfers knowledge between them to accelerate learning. The online organization makes the sequence of tasks part of the learning process, giving earlier experience a role in the broader training procedure.

The approach comes with theoretical guarantees, and experiments show dramatic learning acceleration across a variety of dynamical systems, including quadrotor control. These findings support knowledge transfer as a way to reduce the experience burden of policy gradient learning in the evaluated settings. The contribution combines sequential multi-task learning with policy optimization, linking a familiar control-learning method to a mechanism for reusing knowledge.
icml-2014-online-multi-task-learning-for.tldr: An online multi-task policy gradient method transfers knowledge across consecutive tasks and substantially accelerates learning in the reported dynamical-system experiments.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis reduces the number of dimensions needed to represent data, and robust variants seek to make that representation less sensitive to problematic observations. This paper identifies a mismatch in the robust PCA methods it discusses: they center data using an L2-based mean even though their objectives use an L1 norm.

The center that suits one distance measure need not be optimal for another. Consequently, calculating the center separately can leave the dimensionality reduction procedure working around a point that does not fit its own objective. The paper proposes robust PCA objectives that incorporate calculation of the mean directly into the dimensionality reduction optimization.

This joint treatment allows the optimal mean to be determined and removed as part of fitting the representation. The authors emphasize that sparsity-inducing norms make this integration nontrivial. Their theoretical analysis and empirical studies show more effective dimensionality reduction than previous robust PCA methods. The contribution is to make centering consistent with the robust objective being optimized.
icml-2014-optimal-mean-robust-principal-.tldr: Jointly optimizing the data center and robust PCA representation resolves an objective mismatch and improves dimensionality reduction in the reported analysis and experiments.

paragraphs: Support vector machines can lose substantial performance when training data are unreliable, including when labels come from crowdsourcing or semi-supervised methods. Robust SVMs address this concern but introduce two linked difficulties: their non-convex objectives make good local solutions hard to obtain, and the influence assigned to outliers must be controlled.

The paper handles these difficulties together through a homotopy approach. It gradually suppresses the influence of outliers and follows a path of local robust SVM solutions, in a process compared with simulated annealing. A theoretical study of solution geometry establishes that this path can be computed efficiently.

Following the path also supports model selection over different degrees of outlier influence. Experiments show that the algorithm tends to find better local solutions than an alternative based on the concave-convex procedure, while allowing stable and efficient model selection. These are qualified empirical advantages among local solutions. The method connects optimization and robustness tuning through a single changing sequence of robust SVM problems.
icml-2014-outlier-path-a-homotopy-algori.tldr: Outlier Path gradually reduces outlier influence while tracking robust SVM solutions, supporting efficient tuning and empirically better local solutions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn about rankings when the learner can ask only pairwise preference questions. The underlying assumption is that a probability distribution generates complete orderings of a fixed collection of items. A pairwise answer therefore supplies partial evidence about a distribution over rankings.

The learner may seek different properties of that distribution: the item most likely to appear first, the most probable complete ranking, or the distribution itself. These targets require different kinds of conclusions from the same restricted form of observation. Learning a likely winner, for example, is a different objective from recovering a full ordering.

Learning proceeds online, with preference information acquired through queries over time. The stated goal is to keep the number of required observations small while guaranteeing a specified level of confidence. Framed around the Mallows case, the work places ranking elicitation within statistical learning: the central problem is how much pairwise information is needed to make reliable claims about uncertain rankings.
icml-2014-preference-based-rank-elicitat.tldr: The paper studies online learning of ranking-distribution properties from pairwise preferences, aiming to minimize observations while maintaining a specified confidence level.

paragraphs: Finding likely configurations in continuous graphical models requires representing possibilities in a potentially enormous space. This paper develops a particle-based max-product algorithm that maintains several distinct hypotheses about posterior modes. Its goal is to preserve useful alternatives while remaining robust to initialization.

At each iteration, stochastic proposals enlarge the hypothesis set at each node, and an efficient selection procedure reduces it again. The selection problem is formulated to minimize errors in later max-product message updates. Diversity follows from preserving these messages, so the method does not require an application-specific distance measure to decide which hypotheses are sufficiently different.

The algorithm also avoids the stochastic resampling steps used in particle sum-product methods, thereby avoiding common degeneracies in which particles collapse onto one hypothesis. Experiments on human pose estimation from single images show significant improvements over previous particle-based algorithms. The contribution is a selection objective that links hypothesis diversity to the accuracy of subsequent inference computations, rather than treating diversity as a separately tuned preference.
icml-2014-preserving-modes-and-messages-.tldr: Selecting particles to preserve max-product messages maintains diverse hypotheses and improves human pose estimation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures agreement between clusterings, but chance can create apparent agreement. Earlier adjustments subtract the expected value and normalize against an upper bound, establishing a constant baseline. This paper argues that choosing among many candidate clusterings creates an additional concern: selection bias.

The proposed standardized mutual information reduces the tendency to prefer candidates with more clusters or fewer data points when comparing them with a reference clustering. It requires the variance of mutual information under a hypergeometric randomness model. The authors derive an analytical formula for this technically challenging quantity and analyze the computational complexity of obtaining it.

Experiments examine how standardization addresses selection bias and improves interpretability. The authors specifically recommend the measure for multiple clustering comparisons when the number of records is small relative to the number of clusters being considered. The contribution distinguishes correcting an average chance baseline from accounting for variability when selecting among alternatives, showing why the latter can matter for interpreting a high agreement score.
icml-2014-standardized-mutual-informatio.tldr: Standardized mutual information uses chance variability to reduce selection bias when comparing many clusterings, especially with few records relative to clusters.

paragraphs: The paper combines deep neural networks with approximate Bayesian inference to construct deep directed generative models. Such models connect hidden variables to observed data, creating a need to learn both how observations are generated and how hidden variables can be inferred from them. The proposed algorithm addresses these linked computations at scale.

A recognition model represents an approximate posterior distribution over hidden variables. Training uses this approximation to optimize a variational lower bound. The authors develop stochastic backpropagation, a set of rules for propagating gradients through stochastic variables, enabling joint optimization of the generative model and the recognition model.

This makes approximate inference a learned component of the overall system. Experiments on several real-world datasets show models that generate realistic samples, accurately fill in missing data, and support visualization of high-dimensional observations. These findings demonstrate several uses of the same framework. The contribution is the combination of a learned posterior approximation with gradient-based joint training through the model’s random variables.
icml-2014-stochastic-backpropagation-and.tldr: Stochastic backpropagation jointly trains deep generative and recognition models, enabling useful generation, missing-data imputation, and visualization.

paragraphs: The paper develops a framework for understanding protein motion from large molecular dynamics simulation datasets. Its design follows three requirements: handling massive amounts of data, respecting relevant physical law, and producing interpretations accessible enough to support protein engineering and drug design. The model uses L1-regularized, reversible hidden Markov models.

The authors present an expectation-maximization algorithm for learning and a model selection criterion based on physical relaxation timescales. This connects the choice of model to the timescales of the protein dynamics being represented. They also implement the algorithm on GPUs and report improved robustness compared with standard biophysics methods.

The framework is applied to two large simulation datasets generated on the NCSA Bluewaters supercomputer and the Folding@Home network. The resulting analysis identifies ubiquitin conformational dynamics responsible for signaling and clarifies the stepwise activation of c-Src kinase. These applications connect the computational design to interpretable molecular behavior, showing how a model built for scale and physical consistency can support analysis of protein mechanisms.
icml-2014-understanding-protein-dynamics.tldr: Reversible, L1-regularized hidden Markov models provide scalable and interpretable analyses of protein dynamics, revealing mechanisms in ubiquitin and c-Src.
